name: Prefixes (Milli, Kilo, Mega...)
description: Standard prefixes that make units bigger or smaller (like kilo-, milli-, mega-)

content.overview: Nobody wants to write 0.001 meters when they could just say 1 millimeter. Nobody wants to write 1000 grams when 'a kilogram' says it in one word. Prefixes are just shortcuts for numbers with a lot of zeros. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Physics loves extremes — atoms are absurdly tiny, galaxies are absurdly huge. If you tried writing out every zero by hand, you'd lose your mind. So scientists agreed on a set of prefixes instead. {{viz:diagram-02}}

A prefix is nothing fancy — it's just a stand-in for a power of 10:

**Going bigger:**
- kilo (k) = ×1,000 = 10³
- mega (M) = ×1,000,000 = 10⁶
- giga (G) = ×1,000,000,000 = 10⁹
- tera (T) = ×1,000,000,000,000 = 10¹²

**Going smaller:**
- centi (c) = ÷100 = 10⁻²
- milli (m) = ÷1,000 = 10⁻³
- micro (μ) = ÷1,000,000 = 10⁻⁶
- nano (n) = ÷1,000,000,000 = 10⁻⁹
- pico (p) = ÷1,000,000,000,000 = 10⁻¹²

**Real examples you've probably already used:** {{viz:chart-01}}
- 1 kilometer (km) = 1,000 meters — not a million, just a thousand
- 1 millimeter (mm) = 0.001 meters
- 1 microgram (μg) = 0.000001 grams
- 1 nanosecond (ns) = 0.000000001 seconds

And the prefix always sits right in front of the unit, no exceptions. {{viz:anim-01}}

**Why go to the trouble?**
- It's faster to write: 5 km beats writing 5,000 m
- It's easier to read at a glance: 2 mm beats 0.002 m
- The name matches the vibe: 'milli' sounds tiny, 'kilo' sounds substantial
- You pick the prefix that fits what you're measuring — nanometers for atoms, kilometers for road trips.
keyPoints: A prefix is just a stand-in for a power of 10
mega-, giga-, and tera- are your go-to prefixes for huge numbers
content.whyItMatters: Prefixes show up on almost every measurement you'll ever read. Once they click, a label like '5 μg' instantly makes sense instead of looking like alphabet soup.
